extraction.name: CoNLL-2003 named entity data
extraction.description: Language-independent named entity recognition dataset for English and German with training, development, test, and unannotated files, annotated for four entity types: persons, locations, organizations, and miscellaneous names.
extraction.creator: Erik F. Tjong Kim Sang and Fien De Meulder
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The English data was taken from the Reuters Corpus and the German data was extracted from the ECI Multilingual Text Corpus, specifically the German newspaper Frankfurter Rundshau. The dataset includes training, development, test, and large unannotated files for each language.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Reuters news stories for English and articles from the German newspaper Frankfurter Rundshau in the ECI Multilingual Text Corpus for German.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: English: Reuters news stories between August 1996 and August 1997; training/development from end of August 1996; test from December 1996; raw data from September 1996. German: training/development/test from one week at the end of August 1992; raw data from September to December 1992.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A tokenizer, part-of-speech tagger, and chunker were applied to all data. Two language-specific tokenizers were created; English was tagged and chunked with MBT, and German was lemmatized, tagged, and chunked with TreeTagger.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Named entity tagging for English and German training, development, and test data was done manually at the University of Antwerp, mostly following MUC conventions, with an additional MISC category for names not in the other categories.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The dataset assumes named entities are non-recursive and non-overlapping; when a named entity is embedded in another, usually only the top-level entity is annotated.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The MISC category is very diverse, and when a named entity is embedded in another named entity, usually only the top-level entity is annotated.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development/tuning, testing, and incorporating unannotated data into the learning process for named entity recognition systems.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: The English data was taken from the Reuters Corpus2. The text for the German data was taken from the ECI Multilingual Text Corpus3. Named entity tagging of English and German training, development, and test data, was done by hand at the University of Antwerp.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: The English data was taken from the Reuters Corpus2. This corpus consists of Reuters news stories between August 1996 and August 1997. The text for the German data was taken from the ECI Multilingual Text Corpus3. This corpus consists of texts in many languages. The portion of data that was used for this task, was extracted from the German newspaper Frankfurter Rundshau.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: This corpus consists of Reuters news stories between August 1996 and August 1997. For the training and development set, ten days’ worth of data were taken from the files representing the end of August 1996. For the test set, the texts were from December 1996. The preprocessed raw data covers the month of September 1996. All three of the training, development and test sets were taken from articles written in one week at the end of August 1992. The raw data were taken from the months of September to December 1992.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: The participants were given access to the corpus after some linguistic preprocessing had been done: for all data, a tokenizer, part-of-speech tagger, and a chunker were applied to the raw data. We created two basic language-specific tokenizers for this shared task. The English data was tagged and chunked by the memory-based MBT tagger (Daelemans et al., 2002). The German data was lemmatized, tagged and chunked by the decision tree tagger Treetagger (Schmid, 1995).

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Named entity tagging of English and German training, development, and test data, was done by hand at the University of Antwerp. Mostly, MUC conventions were followed (Chinchor et al., 1999). An extra named entity category called MISC was added to denote all names which are not already in the other categories.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: We assume that named entities are non-recursive and non-overlapping. When a named entity is embedded in another named entity, usually only the top level entity has been annotated.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: The English data was tagged and chunked by the memory-based MBT tagger (Daelemans et al., 2002). The German data was lemmatized, tagged and chunked by the decision tree tagger Treetagger (Schmid, 1995).

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: An extra named entity category called MISC was added to denote all names which are not already in the other categories. This includes adjectives, like Italian , and events, like 1000 Lakes Rally , making it a very diverse category. When a named entity is embedded in another named entity, usually only the top level entity has been annotated.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: For each of the languages there is a training file, a development file, a test file and a large file with unannotated data. The leaming methods were trained with the training data. The development data could be used for tuning the parameters of the leaming methods. The challenge of this year’s shared task was to incorporate the unannotated data in the leaming process in one way or another.
